You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test case `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass` in `SummaryStatisticsTest` shows that after setting a new `Mean` implementation via `setMeanImpl(new Mean())`, the computed mean using `stats.getMean()` should equal the mean computed by a standalone `Mean` instance applied to the same data array.

The method `setMeanImpl(StorelessUnivariateStatistic meanImpl)` in `SummaryStatistics` replaces the current mean implementation but calls the private method `checkEmpty()` before doing so. `checkEmpty()` throws an exception if any values have already been added (i.e., if n > 0). This means that in order to override the mean implementation, the `SummaryStatistics` instance must have no stored data yet, which the test satisfies by calling `setMeanImpl` before adding values.

When adding values using `addValue(double value)`, the code increments several statistics including sum, sumsq, min, max, sumLog, the second moment, and conditionally increments the mean, variance, and geometric mean only if the respective implementations are not the default ones (`Mean`, `Variance`, `GeometricMean`). Thus, if the mean implementation is the default `Mean`, no separate incrementing for `meanImpl` occurs in `addValue`.

`getMean()` simply returns `meanImpl.getResult()`.

Relating to the current bug report about `setVarianceImpl` affecting `getStandardDeviation` to produce NaN:

Similarly, `setVarianceImpl(StorelessUnivariateStatistic varianceImpl)` also calls `checkEmpty()` to ensure no data was yet added before replacement, then replaces the variance calculation implementation.

`getStandardDeviation()` depends on `getVariance()` (returns `varianceImpl.getResult()`) and takes the square root if count > 1.

If the variance implementation is replaced by a new `Variance` instance just before any data is added (so no exception thrown), then when values are added, the `addValue` method checks if `varianceImpl` is not the default `Variance`, then increments the variance implementation. Since the replaced variance is a new instance, it will be incremented correctly.

The issue arises if the variance implementation is replaced *after* data has been added (which the `checkEmpty` method disallows and should throw an error) or if the variance implementation is replaced with a `Variance` instance that is not correctly reset or updated before getting the standard deviation. The code for getting standard deviation relies on `varianceImpl.getResult()` which might return NaN if variance is not properly calculated.

Thus, the root cause is that after replacing the variance implementation or mean implementation by `setVarianceImpl` or `setMeanImpl`, the existing stored values are not reprocessed/replayed against the new implementation, so the internal state is inconsistent. The design requires replacing these implementations only before adding data, otherwise the new implementation starts empty/not updated and subsequent getters return incorrect (NaN) results.

The failing test `testOverrideMeanWithMathClass` passes because it does replace the mean implementation before adding values, so the new mean is properly incremented. But the bug report shows usage that replaces variance implementation and then adds values, but the setup and verification might be problematic if the new variance is not incremented or results in NaN.

Summary:
- The `setMeanImpl` and `setVarianceImpl` methods require that no data is added before replacing the implementation (enforced by `checkEmpty`)
- The `addValue` method increments the current implementations accordingly only if they differ from the default
- The bug in the variance case might happen if the variance implementation is replaced improperly or if the user ignores `checkEmpty` or forcibly replaces it after data was added
- The design does not support replacing implementations after data is added because no replay of previously added values occurs
- This lack of replay/update is why `getStandardDeviation` may return NaN if the variance implementation reports NaN due to missing data or internal state

No recent bug reports seem relevant to this specific behavioral contract.

Hence the cause of the problem is misuse of replacing variance or other implementations after data is added without resetting or replaying previous values, which leads to inconsistent internal state and NaN results.

This diagnosis matches the code behavior and bug report symptoms.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
